newsitem.title: USA: Brennan's coffin brought to U.S. Supreme Court.
newsitem.headline: Brennan's coffin brought to U.S. Supreme Court.

text.p: William Brennan's closed, flag-draped coffin was brought to the Supreme Court Monday as his former colleagues, family and others mourned the death of one of the most influential jurists in U.S. history.

On a sweltering, overcast day, Brennan's casket was carried up the court's marbled steps across from the U.S. Capitol by 10 pallbearers who had worked as law clerks for the legendary liberal whose rulings expanded the rights of most Americans.

Once the casket was brought inside the Supreme Court's Great Hall, it was placed on a historic catafalque -- the same one used in 1865 for the assassinated President Abraham Lincoln -- for a day of lying-in-state.

Three of the nine current Supreme Court members, two retired colleagues, Brennan's wife, his three children and numerous court employees attended a brief ceremony before the hall was opened for public viewing.
A Catholic priest, Milton Jordan, referred to Brennan's accomplishments during 34 years on the nation's highest court. "This was his life. This was his way of touching our lives," he said.
Brennan, who retired from the bench in 1990 after suffering a stroke, died Thursday after a long illness. Brennan, 91, had been in failing health for some time.

On the court, Brennan wrote landmark rulings that expanded the rights of minorities and women; led to the reapportionment of voting districts to guarantee the ideal of "one person, one vote," and gave free-speech protection to the news media.

Brennan joined three colleagues -- Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall, a civil rights legend, and former Chief Justices Earl Warren and Warren Burger -- as the only high court members whose caskets have lain in state.
Those attending the ceremony were liberal Justices John Paul Stevens and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, conservative Clarence Thomas and retired Justices Harry Blackmun and Byron White.
A Supreme Court spokeswoman said the other six court members were out-of-town. The court is in the midst of its regular summer recess.

Several hundred people lined up outside the Supreme Court building. A visiting law student from Ohio cited Brennan's "impact on the law" while the father of a vacationing New Jersey family called Brennan "obviously a very important man."

A Supreme Court police official said he did not expect the same huge crowds for Brennan as for Marshall in 1993, when thousands of people came to pay homage to a hero of the U.S. civil rights movement and first black on the high court.

Brennan's funeral will be held Tuesday at St. Matthew's Cathedral in Washington, D.C. Among those expected to deliver eulogies are President Clinton, Brennan's successor, Justice David Souter, and his son William.
